docs.title: SAFE4SOC Information Sharing Gateway
docs.text:
This is the documentation of the GitHub project SAFE4SOC-Gateway.

The SAFE4SOC Information Sharing Gateway (S4S-IS-GW) is a cybersecurity software component developed within the European research and innovation project SAFE4SOC, funded under the EU Digital Europe Programme.

Its primary purpose is to enable secure, interoperable, and automated exchange of cybersecurity information between different organizations and security infrastructures, particularly Security Operations Centers (SOCs).

The gateway acts as an intermediary between cybersecurity systems, allowing them to exchange security alerts and incident-related information while enforcing configurable security and information-sharing policies.

docs.title: Key objectives
docs.text:
1. Interoperability: Facilitate standardized cybersecurity information exchange using the Incident Detection Message Exchange Format version 2 (IDMEFv2).
  2. Secure communication: Protect exchanged information through encrypted communication and mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication.
  3. Information filtering: Apply configurable policies to determine which cybersecurity information may be shared with other organizations.
  4. Data validation: Validate exchanged security alerts against predefined JSON schemas to ensure structural correctness and interoperability.
  5. Integration: Connect existing SOC infrastructures and security monitoring systems without requiring major changes to their internal architectures.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The gateway consists of a sender gateway on the sender side and the receiving gateway on the receiver side (denoted in blue). As database for storing the received alert messages Kafka is used (denoted in orange). Kafka does not natively support JSON objects send via HTTP REST, therefore a translation was provided by the Kafka developers to translate HTTP Rest API calls into native Kafka protocol communication.

The sender gateway receives IDMEFv2 as JSON formatted alert message via HTTP message. The gateway sender afterward performs configured checking, filtering, or enrichment and forwards the alert to the receiver side gateway. Here the alert is also checked, filtered or enriched as configured and afterward sent to the Kafka HTTP Rest API container. The Kafka REST API container does the translation to the final destination, the Kafka database which is locally reachable on the receiver side.

docs.title: Compilation
docs.text: The project is configured for the IDE Intellij Community Edition. The project uses Spring Boot, however it is compiled using GraalVM to produce an executable with faster startup times and less memory footprint during execution.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: To create the image, run the following gradlew build command. For installation instructions please see - Docker and docker-compose must be installed beforehand - Install GraalVM https://www.graalvm.org/latest/getting-started/ (NOTE: GraalVM 21.0.2 is working. GraalVM 25+ is not working!) - Install gcc glibc-devel zlib-devel etc. https://www.graalvm.org/latest/reference-manual/native-image/

docs.title: GraalVM Installation Via SDKMAN (a simplified option)
docs.text:
Install SDKMAN. 

curl -s "https://get.sdkman.io" | bash
source ~/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh
Download and switch to GraalVM. 
sdk install java 21.0.2-graalce
sdk use java 21.0.2-graalce

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
java -version
echo $GRAALVM_HOME 
echo $JAVA_HOME
should show: GraalVM CE 21.x.x and both variables need to show to the installed GraalVM directory on your machine. If not you need to configure your local Java setup. Please note, do not use Graal VM 25 or above as it is not compatible with the Java-version used.

docs.title: Building Instructions Using IntelliJ IDEA
docs.text:
The project can be opened using IntelliJ IDEA and the Spring Boot application can be launched and debugged directly using the run configuration profiles stored in folder ".run" in the project's root directory. One profile is used for the sender role and one for the receiver role.

If natively launched within IntelliJ's execution, the behavior is the same as for the build using GraalVM, however, the startup time is slower and debugging is simplified.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The gateway must be configured using the file application.properties which is available under path ./src/main/resources. Please note that a copy of the contents of this resources folder in embedded into the GraalVM binary, in any case and must be overloaded using an external configuration file via docker volume as shown in the corresponding docker compose files.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Different configuration profiles were developed for configuration and testing within IntelliJ IDEA for sender and receiver. The corresponding files are:

  • application.properties (main default config for debugging directly in IntelliJ IDEA)
  • application-receiver.properties
  • application-sender.properties
  • application-tls-in-on.properties (profile that activates incoming tls config)
  • application-tls-out-on.properties (profile that activates outgoing tls config)
  • docker.properties (is loaded externally docker-compose script.)

Please edit config in docker-compose file as otherwise the config will be overwritten.

docs.title: Gateway Role
docs.text:
This switch lets the gateway act as sending gateway. Options are either SENDER or RECEIVER. 

gatewayRole=SENDER

docs.title: Sender Gateway Properties
docs.text:
These entries specify the destination domain and port of the receiving gateway where messages must be forwarded to.

gatewayDomainRC=localhost
gatewayPortRC=8081

These entries specify self-information for the gateway, needed for alert entry enrichment, for instance. 

gatewayDomainSD=localhost
gatewayPortSD=8080

docs.title: Receiver Gateway Properties
docs.text:
These entries identify where the local Kafka database can be found. 

kafkaDomainLocal=kafkalocal
kafkaPortLocal=8082

docs.title: SSL Activation or Deactivation (DEBUG Connection Settings)
docs.text:
The gateway has a setting to control the inbound SSL configuration (Spring boot VM settings), and the outbound SSL configuration (Java internal SSL Context object). Both can be activated or deactivated separately using the following flags in docker-compose.

      GATEWAY_PROTOCOL: https     # for communication from gateway sender to gateway receiver
      SSL_INBOUND_ACTIVATED: true
      SSL_OUTBOUND_ACTIVATED: true

For debug purposes in a testing environment the SSL-settings can be both be set to false. This means that neither the initial connection from the outside inside the Gateway-sender nor the forwarding from Gateway-sender to Geteway-receiver will apply HTTPS but only HTTP. This setting is not acceptable for a production environment but ONLY FOR TESTING PURPOSES!

The file docker-compose-debug-http.yaml is properly configured to work out of the box and can be launched using:

docker compose up -d rest-proxy control-center schema-registry broker 
docker compose -f docker-compose-debug-http.yaml up gateway-sender
docker compose -f docker-compose-debug-http.yaml up gateway-receiver

docs.title: Relevant Headers
docs.text:
For information purposes the outgoing requests hold the role information as HTTP Headers. This array lists headers to be forwarded within the gateway. All other headers are dropped. 

relevantHeaders={'content-type','accept','user-Agent','accept-Encoding','safe4soc-receiver-hostname','safe4soc-receiver-port'}

docs.title: Additional Endpoints for Debugging
docs.text:
If configuration testing is required the following endpoints can be used to reload a configuration during runtime. However, they MUST BE DEACTIVATED in secure mode using the corresponding flags: 

endpoints.reloadconfig.enabled: false
endpoints.setisa.enabled: false

docs.title: Information Sharing Agreement Configuration
docs.text:
The entry about the ISA is very important, as it contains the configuration about necessary filtering, enrichment, required fields, and alert drop instructions. If no external ISA.json file is found under the specified "isaPath" by default a standard ISA embedded into the GraalVM compiled binary will be used.

docs.title: Filter Configuration
docs.text:
The Filtering configuration uses a nested list in JSON format. Scalar filter rules use the configured replacement value. For an empty string (""), the gateway checks a candidate alert against the configured schema. It omits the field if the empty string introduces a validation error. An empty object clears the contents of the corresponding object or array for supported nested filters. For Analyzer, Sensor, Source, and Target, a blank rule applies to the named field and preserves the rest of the entry. A nonempty string rule for Sensor, Source, or Target replaces the existing IP addresses in the array. The gateway validates the alert against the configured IDMEFv2 schema before ISA processing and again after filtering and enrichment. If either validation fails, the gateway returns HTTP 422 and stops forwarding.

  "filterConfig": {
    "CreateTime": "",
    "StartTime": ""
  },

docs.title: Enrichment
docs.text:
The enrichment configuration uses a nested list in JSON format, also. However, each enrichment functionality must be implemented specifically. The class Utils contains a prepared nested case structure for all elements to individually implement an enrichment where necessary.

  "enrichmentConfig": {\
    "CreateTime": "",\
    "StartTime": ""\
  }\
}

Currently, the feature is available to enrich alerts with missing timestamps. If it is missing the timestamp within the running gateway will be used as value in the same format for the CreateTime or StartTime field.

docs.title: Drop Configuration
docs.text:
This JSON element inside the ISA lists elements that cause the forwarding of alerts to be completely dropped and aborted. If values that are configured here are found in an IDMEFv2 alert, the dropping is triggered.

  "dropConfig": {
    "Version": "",
    "ID": "",
    "Status": "",
    "OrganisationName": "",
    "CreateTime": "",
    "StartTime": "",
    "Cause": "",
    "Category": "",
    "Priority": "High",
    "Confidence": "",
    "Description": ""
  },

As can be seen above, these fields can be used for drop configuration. If an alert is processed with a priority value "High" it will NOT be forwarded, but dropped.

docs.title: Required Configuration
docs.text:
This JSON element inside the ISA lists elements that that must be non-empty values, otherwise the forwarding will be aborted. Please note this is distìnguished from filtering configuration.

  "requiredConfig": {
    "Version": "",
    "ID": "",
    "StartTime": "",
    "Status": "",
    "Source": "",
    "Target": ""
  }

docs.title: Demonstration
docs.text:
To fully demonstrate how alerts are sent to Kafka through the gateway following commands are necessary. The Kafka GitHub project provides docker samples for all their services running out the box. Their sample was taken from here: https://docs.confluent.io/platform/current/get-started/platform-quickstart.html. The docker sample was taken from here: https://github.com/confluentinc/cp-all-in-one/tree/7.9.0-post/cp-all-in-one/docker-compose.yml

The gateways were added to the docker compose file located in the root folder of the project. It can be launched via: 

docker-compose up -d rest-proxy control-center schema-registry broker gateway-receiver gateway-sender
Please note more services are included in the sample file, such as flink or ksqldb but for the demo they are not needed.

After about a minute the system should be launched and the Kafka dashboard can be reached via web browser at 

localhost:9021
You should see something similar to this: Landing page

Click on controlcenter.cluster

Click on Topics

Click on alerts (if it was already set up correctly). If it is not there yet you can either send the first message via curl or click on the GUI "Add topic" at the top right.

Click on messages to see the current stored messages.

Please note that for Kafke message consumption each message requires a key, in this case it was "test" and the IDMEFv2 alert is stored inside the value filed of the JSON message. docs.title: Compilation of Project Documentation
docs.text:
Use these commands to update the documentation

docker compose -f docker-compose.docs.yml run --rm mkdocs build
The resulting files are placed in site/.

docs.title: Automatically publish to GitHub Pages
docs.text:
Create .github/workflows/documentation.yml: 

name: Publish Documentation

on:
push:
branches:
- main
paths:
- "docs/**"
- "mkdocs.yml"
- ".github/workflows/documentation.yml"
workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
contents: write

jobs:
deploy:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install MkDocs
        run: pip install "mkdocs-material==9.*"

      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
        run: mkdocs gh-deploy --force

This builds the documentation and pushes the generated website to the gh-pages branch.
